interpretations.rationale: The question was whether LeadershipTransferToServer reports a transfer that the named server can complete when that server is a non-voter, and what happens to leadership while it cannot. The execution answers the first half directly. In the control case naming a voter (parsed indices 0 and 1) the call returned nil and the requested server was Leader at the endpoint while the previous leader was Follower, so the call does perform real transfers. In the case naming the non-voter (parsed indices 2 and 3, setup event index 2 matched as admission) the same call returned nil while the requested server was never observed as Leader within 1500ms and finished as Follower; the previous leader was not Leader at the endpoint and the maximum term across the cluster had risen from 2 to 4, with the same server holding leadership at term 4, which a Raft leader cannot do without having stepped down and won a later election. The source explains the mechanism as predicted. The leader resolves the requested ID only through leaderState.replState, which startStopReplication populates for every configured server except the leader without consulting Suffrage, so a non-voter passes and receives TimeoutNow; timeoutNow sets it to Candidate and marks candidateFromLeadershipTransfer, a flag that by design suppresses pre-vote, so it sends a real RequestVote carrying the next term. Each voter adopts the higher term and becomes a follower before reaching the hasVote check, which then refuses the vote because the candidate holds no vote, so the requested server can never collect a grant. The old leader learns of the higher term, steps down, and its transfer goroutine reports success from the leftLeaderLoop branch, so the caller is told the transfer succeeded while leadership has in fact left it for a server it did not choose, or returned to it in a later term. That mismatch is the defect: for the documented purpose of handing leadership over, a success result that the named target can never satisfy leaves the caller unable to distinguish a completed handover from a self-inflicted leadership interruption. The liveness side is bounded rather than unbounded and this receipt does not measure it, since leadership was sampled only at the end of the observation window; the revised probe samples every millisecond and records the leaderless samples. No data loss is claimed: committed entries stay committed and a voter is elected afterwards.

interpretations.rationale: The documented purpose of LeadershipTransferToServer is to transition leadership to a specific server in the cluster, and the only target validation in the leader is a lookup in leaderState.replState, which holds an entry for every configured server except the leader regardless of Suffrage; a missing entry is the sole error. The account is asserted on that source basis and stays conditional until the requested two-case probe reports what the call returns versus which server actually takes leadership; the controlling contrast is the same call naming a voter, and the note that auto-targeted LeadershipTransfer() skips non-voters via pickServer shows the library itself does not consider a non-voter a valid transfer target when it chooses.

The question was whether its success establishes voter-majority contact; the execution says it does not. In the retained run of the three-partition probe, the leader whose only reachable peer was the non-voter returned success in 0ms while its own latest configuration reported three voters, one non-voter and a quorum size of 2, and the leader was still in Leader state (parsed event index 1); the control partition that kept one voter reachable also returned success, which shows the harness does observe a genuine acknowledgement path (index 3); the control partition with no reachable peer did not return success at all, returning 'leadership lost while committing log' after 202ms with the node in Follower state, so the leader cannot reach the threshold on its own vote and the non-voter acknowledgement is what satisfied it in the first case (index 5). All three declared comparisons hold with the setup event matched as admission (correlations 1->0, 3->2, 5->4). The source explains the mechanism: verifyLeader asks every entry of leaderState.replState to acknowledge, startStopReplication creates such an entry for every configured server except the leader without consulting Suffrage, any successful AppendEntries or InstallSnapshot reply from such a peer calls notifyAll(true) and increments verifyFuture.votes, and the threshold compared against is quorumSize(), counted over voters alone. The same package treats voter eligibility strictly in its other leadership tests: checkLeaderLease does not count a non-voter, requestVote refuses a candidate that holds no vote, and quorumSize itself counts only voters, so the verify path is the outlier rather than a deliberate relaxation. The consequence for reads stays bounded and is not what this receipt measures. The leader's lease is voter-only, and both Config.Validate and ReloadConfig enforce LeaderLeaseTimeout <= HeartbeatTimeout <= ElectionTimeout, so the old leader is normally removed before a voter majority elects a successor; the no-peer control is exactly that lease firing at 202ms with a 200ms lease. What the receipt does establish is the weaker but unconditional part: for an interval in which the leader exchanged nothing with any other voter, VerifyLeader reports success, so a caller relying on that call for read consistency is really relying on the lease timer rather than on the acknowledgements VerifyLeader collected. The same file shows the omission is not a considered relaxation of voter eligibility: electSelf and preElectSelf build the very same voter-sized threshold, and both iterate the leader's latest configuration asking only servers whose Suffrage is Voter, so a candidate neither solicits nor counts a non-voter's grant even though nothing on the granting side stops a non-voter from granting a vote if it were asked. Only the verify path asks every replication peer. That contrast is recorded as its own Behaviour so the finding is not reused without it, and it turns the question's answer from 'the success signal is weaker than its documentation' into 'the success signal contradicts the eligibility rule the same decisions use everywhere else'.

d704b04e706144dc964ff451359eda19-gap-0.explanation: Still unresolved, but now bounded from both sides. The grant side closes what the previous answer left open: a voter rejects a vote request while it still knows a leader other than the candidate (raft.go 1673-1679, and the same check on pre-votes at 1786-1792) and clears that knowledge only when its own campaign path runs, which requires HeartbeatTimeout without leader contact (raft.go 227-228). A successor therefore needs a quorum of voters past that trigger, so the earliest successor is HeartbeatTimeout plus the election rounds after the last contact, while the old leader steps down at the first lease check with voter contact age exceeding LeaderLeaseTimeout, at the latest LeaderLeaseTimeout + minCheckInterval (10ms) <= HeartbeatTimeout + 10ms. With the documented defaults the leadership window closes about 500ms before any successor can exist; only an equal-lease configuration leaves a residual of a few milliseconds, and that needs the granters to clear at the earliest instant. What remains untested is whether that residual is reachable at all, and whether a stalled leader goroutine widens it, so the gap stays open as a schedule-dependent condition rather than a configuration-dependent one.

knowledge.assertion: Election vote solicitation asks only servers whose Suffrage is Voter, so the verify path's inclusion of non-voters is an omission rather than the intended eligibility rule.
A follower campaigns after HeartbeatTimeout without leader contact, not after ElectionTimeout, and the leader's lease check granularity is max(10ms, LeaderLeaseTimeout - maxDiff).

counterevidence: checkLeaderLease counts voters only, so a leader that has lost voter-majority contact steps down within about LeaderLeaseTimeout; the no-peer control shows this concretely (leadership lost at 202ms with a 200ms lease), which bounds the stale-read consequence rather than showing the verify decision support to be adequate.

Config.Validate keeps LeaderLeaseTimeout <= HeartbeatTimeout <= ElectionTimeout, and ReloadConfig re-runs ValidateConfig, so a leader cannot be configured to outlive a follower's election timer through the public reload API.

In the non-voter partition the other servers stayed in term 2 with no leader change, so the receipt does not witness a successor being elected while the old leader still verified; that half of the consequence remains unobserved.

The grant side bounds the consequence more tightly than the verify quorum does: because a voter refuses votes while it knows another leader, no successor can be elected before HeartbeatTimeout plus an election round after the last leader contact, while the lease removes the old leader at LeaderLeaseTimeout + minCheckInterval at the latest; with the documented defaults the two cannot overlap, and even when LeaderLeaseTimeout equals HeartbeatTimeout the residual is a few milliseconds.
limitations: Repeatability under the same fixed input is now shown for one additional run: receipt 107a6d6c816d448da2b7ff6e3145bac1 reproduces all three outcomes of receipt b02d5ff23a504a8ea38116085ba8e23c, with the non-voter-only partition returning success in 0ms while the leader stayed Leader, the voter-only control also returning success, and the no-peer partition returning 'leadership lost while committing log' at 208ms against 202ms in the first run. The two step-down times are the schedule-dependent quantity in that control; a repeat under the same timeouts and transports shows reproducibility, not schedule independence or independence from the JIT of the harness.

The stale-read consequence needs a successor elected while the old leader reports verify success, and the two orderings that decide it are both in the source. A voter refuses a vote or a pre-vote while it still knows a leader other than the candidate (raft.go 1673-1679 and 1786-1792), and it clears that knowledge only in its own campaign path, which runs after HeartbeatTimeout without leader contact (raft.go 227-228). A successor therefore needs a quorum of voters that have already reached that trigger, so it cannot exist earlier than HeartbeatTimeout after their last contact with the old leader, plus the election rounds. The leader, meanwhile, steps down at the first lease check whose voter contact age exceeds LeaderLeaseTimeout, and ValidateConfig allows LeaderLeaseTimeout to equal HeartbeatTimeout: in the worst schedule the boundary check still counts the voter (the comparison is diff <= leaseTimeout) and the step-down follows after minCheckInterval = 10ms. So under a validated configuration the leader leaves office in at most LeaderLeaseTimeout + 10ms, which is at most HeartbeatTimeout + 10ms, while no successor can be elected before HeartbeatTimeout plus a round of pre-vote and vote. The residual exposure is therefore confined to configurations with LeaderLeaseTimeout == HeartbeatTimeout and schedules where the granters clear at the earliest instant, and it is a few milliseconds at most; the practical route to a longer exposure is a leader whose own goroutine is stalled or whose clock jumps, which the earlier account relied on.

The probe uses one process with real Raft instances and in-memory transports, so it exercises the leader's own replication and verify paths but not process-level partitions or multi-host clocks; the partition was made by disconnecting transports in both directions.
